beats.text: At Google, AI now generates about seventy-five percent of all new code. Two years ago, it was about a quarter.
beats.dir: intriguing hook, a little ominous

v.label: GOOGLE · SHARE OF NEW CODE GENERATED BY AI

beats.text: So if a machine is writing three out of every four lines, here's the obvious question. What happens to the people who used to write them?
beats.dir: curious, building intrigue

beats.text: Search "will AI replace software engineers", and you'll find two camps. One says coding is dead. The other says nothing will change.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Both are wrong. And the real data tells a much stranger story, one that matters a lot if you work in IT, or you're planning to.
beats.dir: confident, intriguing

beats.text: In the next few minutes, we'll look at what AI can actually do today, who is really losing jobs, what India's IT giants are doing, and the skills that keep you on the right side of this shift.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: First, let's decode that seventy-five percent, because it doesn't mean what most headlines suggest.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Google's CEO said it refers to new code, generated by AI and then reviewed and accepted by engineers. Not the whole codebase. And not code that ships without a human checking it.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Think of it like autocomplete on your phone. If your keyboard suggests three out of four words in a message, you still decided what the message says.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

msgs.text: Running late, I will be there in

beats.text: Microsoft gave a similar picture. Satya Nadella said AI writes twenty to thirty percent of the code in some of its projects.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So AI is clearly typing a lot. But typing was never the hardest part of a software engineer's job.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.text: Typing was never the hard part

beats.text: And here's the twist. Programmers have heard this exact prediction before. Seventy years ago.
beats.dir: leaning in, a twist

beats.text: In 1954, IBM published the first report on a new language called FORTRAN. It promised that FORTRAN would "virtually eliminate coding and debugging".
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Instead of writing raw machine instructions, you could write something close to a maths formula, and the computer would translate it for you.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Did programmers disappear? The opposite. Making programming easier made software cheaper, so the world wanted far more of it.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Every big jump since then, high-level languages, the internet, cloud platforms, made each programmer more productive. And each time, the total number of programmers grew.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Economists have a name for this. When something gets cheaper, we often end up using much more of it. So the real question isn't whether AI makes coding cheaper. It's who gets the new work.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And this is where the data gets uncomfortable.
beats.dir: serious, leaning in

beats.text: Researchers at Stanford tracked payroll records from millions of American workers. Their latest figures show something striking.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Software developers aged twenty-two to twenty-five are employed almost twenty percent less than a few years ago, while developers over thirty actually grew.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.title: US SOFTWARE DEVELOPERS · EMPLOYMENT CHANGE
v.src: Source: Stanford Digital Economy Lab (ADP payroll data) · bar heights illustrative

beats.text: Job postings tell the same story. On Indeed in the US, only about four and a half percent of software job posts in early twenty twenty-six were entry-level. That's the lowest share of any field Indeed tracks.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.label: ENTRY-LEVEL SHARE OF US SOFTWARE JOB POSTS
v.sub: Q1 2026 · lowest of any field Indeed tracks

beats.text: And most of the recent rebound in software hiring, around seventy percent of it, came from senior roles.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.title: WHERE THE HIRING REBOUND WENT
v.src: Source: Indeed Hiring Lab · May 2025 to May 2026

beats.text: So AI isn't replacing software engineers. It's replacing the first rung of the ladder. The simple tickets, the boilerplate, the small bug fixes that juniors used to learn on.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The researchers are careful to say this is a pattern, not proof that AI alone caused it. Interest rates and over-hiring during the pandemic play a part too. But the direction is hard to ignore.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Now let's bring it home, because India runs one of the biggest software workforces on the planet.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: According to Nasscom, the Indian tech industry's revenue grew about six percent last financial year, but jobs grew only about two percent.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: In other words, the industry is earning more without hiring at the same speed. That gap is exactly what automation looks like on a balance sheet.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: TCS, India's largest IT company, cut more than twelve thousand roles in twenty twenty-five as part of a restructuring, and its net headcount fell by over twenty-three thousand in the year.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: But the hiring hasn't stopped. TCS and Infosys together still plan around forty-five thousand fresher hires this year. And within IT, hiring for AI and machine learning roles is growing.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So the door isn't closed. It's moving. Fewer seats for "write this simple module", more for "build and check AI-powered systems".
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Here's a result that surprised almost everyone, including the developers in it.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: In twenty twenty-five, a research group called METR ran a proper experiment. Experienced open-source developers worked on their own projects, sometimes with AI tools, sometimes without.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Before starting, they expected AI to make them about twenty-four percent faster.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The measured result? With AI, they were nineteen percent slower. And afterwards, they still believed AI had sped them up.
beats.dir: surprised, emphatic

beats.text: Why? Reviewing, correcting and re-prompting AI output takes time, especially in large, complex code you already know well.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: To be fair, that study used early twenty twenty-five tools, and the tools have improved a lot since. But it shows something important. AI writes code fast. Making sure that code is right is still human work.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And there's another reason companies still need humans checking every line.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: In twenty twenty-five, the security company Veracode tested more than a hundred AI models on eighty common coding tasks.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: In forty-five percent of the tasks, the AI-written code contained a known security weakness.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Even when there was a safe way and an unsafe way to write the code, the models picked the unsafe way almost half the time.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And the newer, smarter models weren't much better. They got better at writing code that runs, but not at writing code that's safe.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So as AI writes more code, someone has to understand it well enough to spot the hole before an attacker does. That someone is a software engineer.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So what part of the job is safe? Mostly the parts that were never about typing.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Understanding what the customer actually needs, when they can't explain it clearly.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Designing how a big system fits together, so it doesn't collapse when a million users show up.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Judging whether AI-written code is secure, and whether it really does what the business needs.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And taking responsibility when something breaks at two in the morning. An AI can suggest a fix. It can't be accountable for it.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Notice the pattern. AI is great at answering "how do I write this?" Humans are still needed for "what should we build, and is it right?"
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: That's also why the official forecasts are still positive. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics expects software developer jobs to grow about sixteen percent over the next ten years, much faster than average.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.label: US SOFTWARE DEVELOPER JOBS · 2024–2034
v.src: Source: US Bureau of Labor Statistics

beats.text: So if you're a developer, or you want to be one, here's how to stay on the right side of this.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace
beats.chapter: What to do if you're in IT

v.text: 4 moves if you are in IT

beats.text: One. Use AI tools every day, but treat them like a fast junior teammate. Let them draft. You review, test and decide.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.title: 4 MOVES
v.detail: Treat AI like a fast junior teammate

beats.text: Two. Climb above syntax. Learn system design, debugging and reading other people's code. Those skills get more valuable as AI writes more of the code.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Three. Learn the basics of how AI systems work, and how they fail. Companies need people who can build with AI safely.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Four. If you're a fresher, build real projects that show judgement, not just a certificate. Something deployed, used by real people, and explained clearly.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So, will AI replace software engineers? Not the ones who learn to work with it.
beats.dir: confident, warm

v.text: Not the ones who learn to work with it.

beats.text: But it is changing who gets hired, and what they're hired to do. And that change is happening right now, starting with the very first rung of the ladder.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Tell me in the comments: do you use AI at work? Is it making your job easier, or harder?
beats.dir: friendly, inviting

beats.text: And subscribe to TechDecoded with Max for more tech, decoded.
beats.dir: warm, friendly sign-off
